target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and therefore reliably help people vote.
objection: Declaring Election Day a federal/national holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many retail and service jobs still operate on federal holidays; therefore many workers would still not get time away to vote.

target: AG1’s idea that a national holiday would help low-income workers rather than harm them.
objection: Because low-income workers are disproportionately concentrated in private retail and service jobs that may still be scheduled to work on holidays, a holiday would leave their main voting barrier in place and could disadvantage them.

target: AG1’s assumption that an election holiday by itself is a strong turnout reform.
objection: Research and comparative evidence indicate that an election holiday alone is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1’s implication that a holiday is preferable to other reforms.
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration are more direct and reliable ways to improve access than simply making Election Day a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status would not reliably create time off for many voters.
objection: Even without a legal requirement for private employers to close, a federal holiday commonly causes schools and public offices to close and many workplaces to reduce operations or provide flexibility, so a holiday would in practice create time windows for many voters.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would be especially disadvantaged by a holiday.
objection: The objection assumes low-income workers would still be unable to get meaningful time to vote, but a national holiday is a universal calendar change that should also create holiday-based availability for the services and schedules low-income voters rely on.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday should be rejected because it is not the only turnout reform.
objection: Even if other reforms also help turnout, that does not negate the value of removing a direct scheduling barrier; a holiday can still be justified as one useful reform.

target: AG2’s claim that making voting a celebration is not a sufficient reason for the policy.
objection: Framing voting as a celebration is itself a legitimate policy goal because it can elevate civic participation and democratic legitimacy, even if the holiday is not a complete solution to turnout problems.

target: AG2’s idea that broad support and international precedent do not justify the proposal.
objection: The fact that the holiday has bipartisan support and parallels in many OECD countries shows it is politically and socially workable, which counts in favor of adoption rather than rejection.

target: AG2’s claim that school closure does not materially help working parents vote.
objection: For many working parents, especially low-income families, schools provide daytime supervision or childcare; if schools close for Election Day, that reduces a major barrier to voting even when some employers do not provide paid time off.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures from a holiday would reliably reduce childcare and supervision barriers for parents.
objection: A federal/national holiday does not itself require all schools, including private schools and all districts, to close or change schedules, so school-day supervision and childcare constraints would not be reliably reduced for all parents.

target: AG1’s claim that low-income families would reliably benefit from school closures.
objection: Low-income working families depend heavily on school-based supervision and may not be able to count on school closures or schedule changes, so the holiday would not be a dependable childcare improvement for them.

target: AG1’s broader mechanism that school closure alone makes the holiday a reliable access reform.
objection: If the holiday’s key childcare/supervision mechanism varies by local school decisions, then it cannot be counted on to improve voting access reliably.

target: AG2’s claim that school closures are too unreliable to matter.
objection: In practice, federal-holiday designation commonly leads many public schools and often private schools to close or move to non-instructional schedules, making school-related childcare relief predictable for most parents.

target: AG2’s claim that many low-income working parents would still not get meaningful voting time because of work.
objection: A national holiday typically changes workplace scheduling as well, creating predictable time windows and reducing work-related conflicts even without requiring every private employer to close.

target: AG2’s claim that mandatory employer accommodations or automatic registration are the better reforms.
objection: A national holiday still directly reduces scheduling barriers on the election day itself, so it is a reliable access improvement rather than a lesser substitute for other reforms.

target: AG1’s reliance on the idea that a holiday also addresses administrative/logistical barriers.
objection: A national holiday only changes scheduling; it does not directly address administrative or registration barriers, unlike reforms such as automatic voter registration.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday-only approach is sufficiently reliable.
objection: A reform that does not directly address major categories of voting barriers is less reliable than reforms that target both scheduling and administrative/logistical obstacles.

target: AG1’s claim that closing schools for a holiday would solve childcare constraints for low-income parents.
objection: Even if schools close, parents still need alternative childcare during the same daytime voting hours, and for many low-income families that substitute care is costly or unavailable.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would improve voting access for many low-income working parents.
objection: If childcare constraints remain in place during voting hours, then the holiday does not reliably increase parents’ practical ability to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would still not reliably get time off because private employers need not close.
objection: A federal holiday changes the nationwide calendar for schools and workplaces and reduces reliance on employer-by-employer discretion, making reliable time away more likely for low-income hourly workers.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday would remove scheduling barriers without leaving low-income workers without time to vote.
objection: Because private employers are not required to close or give paid time off, many low-income retail and service workers would still be working during voting hours and could lack guaranteed time away to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that work during the day still blocks voting even with absentee options.
objection: Many voters can use absentee or mail voting from home, so not having time away during Election Day hours is not by itself a guaranteed barrier to voting.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not help with absentee/mail voting.
objection: A protected calendar day off can help voters complete and return absentee or mail ballots and related tasks, increasing practical ability to use those methods.

target: AG1’s absentee/mail ballot argument.
objection: Low-income workers may still lack adequate free time around Election Day to complete and return absentee ballots, and holiday timing can also make mail or drop-off submission harder because those channels may operate on reduced schedules.

target: AG2’s claim that OECD precedent does not support the holiday model.
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that election-day voting on a holiday is a widely used and workable model in other advanced democracies.

target: AG2’s inference that a U.S. holiday would not work because private employers are not forced to close.
objection: OECD countries still use weekend or holiday election days despite having private-sector workers with schedule conflicts, so the absence of a universal legal employer-closure rule does not mean low-income voters lack workable voting time.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would likely leave many low-income workers without reliable time to vote.
objection: Given OECD precedent, the inference that a holiday election day cannot provide workable voting time for low-income workers is not supported.
